q: Why are spirals spaced no closer than 25 mm clear?
o: So concrete and aggregate can flow between the turns
Because spirals cannot be bent tighter
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (Sec. 410 columns; 422.4 axial strength; 425.7 ties and spirals)
n: The clear spacing of spirals is kept between 25 and 75 mm: wide enough for concrete to pass, close enough to confine the core.

q: What does the spiral volumetric ratio ρs measure?
o: The area of longitudinal steel divided by the gross area
The volume of spiral steel divided by the volume of the core it confines
The pitch of the spiral divided by its diameter
The weight of steel per metre of column
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (Sec. 410 columns; 422.4 axial strength; 425.7 ties and spirals)
n: ρs = volume of spiral per turn / volume of core per pitch = 4as(Dc − ds)/(s Dc²). It must reach a minimum so the core stays confined after the shell spalls.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what minimum tie size is needed for a column with 36 mm longitudinal bars?
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (Sec. 410 columns; 422.4 axial strength; 425.7 ties and spirals)
n: Longitudinal bars up to 32 mm take 10 mm ties; 36 mm and larger bars, or bundles, take 12 mm ties.

q: A tied column 300 mm × 300 mm has 16 mm bars and 10 mm ties. What is the maximum tie spacing?
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (Sec. 410 columns; 422.4 axial strength; 425.7 ties and spirals)
n: Take the smallest of 16 × 16 = 256 mm, 48 × 10 = 480 mm and 300 mm. 256 mm governs, usually rounded down to 250 mm on drawings.

q: In concrete design, what does f'c stand for?
o: The specified compressive strength of concrete
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (Sec. 410 columns; 422.4 axial strength; 425.7 ties and spirals)
n: f'c is the 28-day cylinder strength the design is based on, for example 21, 28 or 35 MPa. fy is the steel yield strength.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what is the maximum design axial strength of a tied column?
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (Sec. 410 columns; 422.4 axial strength; 425.7 ties and spirals)
n: The 0.80 factor covers accidental eccentricity in tied columns; spiral columns use 0.85 with φ = 0.75 because spirals give more ductility. The bracket is the concrete plus steel squash load.

q: What do ties and spirals do for a column?
o: They carry most of the axial load in place of the bars
They resist wind uplift on the roof
They hold the longitudinal bars in place and confine the core concrete
They anchor the column to the beam above
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (Sec. 410 columns; 422.4 axial strength; 425.7 ties and spirals)
n: Lateral steel stops the main bars from buckling and squeezes the core, raising its strength and letting it deform more before failure. That is why seismic columns need closely spaced hoops at their ends.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what is the minimum spiral ratio ρs?
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (Sec. 410 columns; 422.4 axial strength; 425.7 ties and spirals)
n: The minimum ρs makes the confined core strong enough to replace the strength lost when the cover shell spalls, so the column does not lose capacity at failure.

q: What minimum tie size does NSCP 2015 require for a column with bundled longitudinal bars?
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (Sec. 410 columns; 422.4 axial strength; 425.7 ties and spirals)
n: Bundled bars act like one large bar, so they need 12 mm ties, the same as 36 mm and larger bars.

q: A column uses 12 mm ties. What limit does the tie size alone put on the tie spacing?
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (Sec. 410 columns; 422.4 axial strength; 425.7 ties and spirals)
n: Spacing may not exceed 48 tie diameters: 48 × 12 = 576 mm. The other two limits (16 bar diameters and the least column dimension) usually govern.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what are the limits on longitudinal steel in an ordinary column?
o: At least 0.5% and at most 4% of the gross area
At least 2% and at most 10% of the gross area
At least 1% and at most 8% of the gross area
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (Sec. 410 columns; 422.4 axial strength; 425.7 ties and spirals)
n: NSCP 410.6.1.1 sets 0.01Ag ≤ Ast ≤ 0.08Ag. Columns of special moment frames are held to 6% (418.7.4.1) so bars fit at splices and the concrete can be placed. In practice 1 to 4% is common.

q: In column design, what is Pn?
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (Sec. 410 columns; 422.4 axial strength; 425.7 ties and spirals)
n: Pn is the computed capacity before the reduction factor. φPn is the design strength, and Pu is the factored load it must at least equal.

q: How does a spiral column fail compared with a tied column?
o: More gradually, since the confined core keeps carrying load
More suddenly, with no warning at all
In exactly the same way as a tied column
By buckling of the spiral wire itself
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (Sec. 410 columns; 422.4 axial strength; 425.7 ties and spirals)
n: When the cover of a spiral column spalls, the confined core still holds up the load and deforms a lot before collapse. Tied columns fail more abruptly, which is why they get lower α and φ values.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what is the minimum clear spacing between turns of a spiral?
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (Sec. 410 columns; 422.4 axial strength; 425.7 ties and spirals)
n: Spirals must be at least 25 mm and no more than 75 mm apart clear. Less blocks the concrete; more gives too little confinement.

q: How do seismic columns differ from the ordinary tie rules?
o: They need no ties at all
They may use wider tie spacing than ordinary columns
They need closely spaced hoops at their ends
They use only 90° hooks on their ties
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (Sec. 410 columns; 422.4 axial strength; 425.7 ties and spirals)
n: Columns in special moment frames need hoops at close spacing over a length lo at each end, where plastic hinges form, with 135° seismic hooks. The ordinary 16db / 48dtie / least-dimension rule is not enough there.

q: A tied column is 250 mm × 400 mm with 20 mm bars and 10 mm ties. Which limit governs the tie spacing?
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (Sec. 410 columns; 422.4 axial strength; 425.7 ties and spirals)
n: The limits are 16 × 20 = 320 mm, 48 × 10 = 480 mm and 250 mm. The least dimension, 250 mm, is the smallest and governs.

q: A column uses 25 mm bars and 20 mm aggregate. What minimum clear spacing between longitudinal bars applies?
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (Sec. 410 columns; 422.4 axial strength; 425.7 ties and spirals)
n: The clear spacing must be at least the largest of 1.5db = 37.5 mm, 40 mm and 4/3 of the aggregate size = 26.7 mm. 40 mm governs.

q: In strength design, how must Pu and φPn compare?
o: Pu must be at least φPn
φPn must be at least Pu
Pu must be at least twice φPn
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (Sec. 410 columns; 422.4 axial strength; 425.7 ties and spirals)
n: Pu is the factored load the column must carry; φPn is its design strength. The design is safe when φPn ≥ Pu.

q: What is a tied column?
o: A column wrapped in a continuous steel helix
A steel column encased in concrete
A column with separate ties at intervals
A column with no longitudinal bars
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (Sec. 410 columns; 422.4 axial strength; 425.7 ties and spirals)
n: Tied columns use closed ties at set spacing and may be square, rectangular or round. Spiral columns use a continuous helix, usually in a round section.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what is the maximum clear spacing between turns of a spiral?
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (Sec. 410 columns; 422.4 axial strength; 425.7 ties and spirals)
n: Spirals must be no more than 75 mm apart clear, or the core would bulge out between turns. The minimum is 25 mm.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what is the minimum diameter of a cast-in-place spiral?
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (Sec. 410 columns; 422.4 axial strength; 425.7 ties and spirals)
n: Cast-in-place spirals must be at least 10 mm in diameter so they are stiff enough to hold their shape during concreting and to confine the core.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what minimum tie size is needed for a column with 25 mm longitudinal bars?
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (Sec. 410 columns; 422.4 axial strength; 425.7 ties and spirals)
n: Bars of 32 mm and smaller take at least 10 mm ties.

q: Under NSCP 2015, how far may an unsupported column bar be from a laterally supported bar?
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (Sec. 410 columns; 422.4 axial strength; 425.7 ties and spirals)
n: Every corner bar and alternate bar sits in a tie corner, and no unsupported bar may be more than 150 mm clear from a supported one. Otherwise crossties are added.

q: In strength design, what is φ?
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (Sec. 410 columns; 422.4 axial strength; 425.7 ties and spirals)
n: φ reduces nominal strength to cover variations in materials, dimensions and workmanship, and it is lower for less ductile failure modes: 0.90 for bending, 0.75 for shear and spiral columns, 0.65 for tied columns.

q: What is a spiral column?
o: A column confined by a continuous steel helix
A column with separate square ties at intervals
A column shaped like a spiral stair
A column reinforced with bundled bars only
ref: NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (Sec. 410 columns; 422.4 axial strength; 425.7 ties and spirals)
n: The continuous spiral confines the round core evenly, so spiral columns are tougher and are given higher α (0.85) and φ (0.75) values than tied columns.
